title: T1071.005 — Application Layer Protocol - Publish/Subscribe Protocols
subtitle: The story: a lobby camera gets an implant through a default password, then listens on an attacker MQTT broker.
aria: T1071.005 - Application Layer Protocol - Publish/Subscribe Protocols

nodes.label: Sensitive data
nodes.tip: Sensitive data - What is at risk

steps.title: Weak door
steps.caption: The attacker logs in to the lobby camera IOT-CAM-17 (192.168.8.34) with the default admin password, which was never changed. The camera sits on a flat IoT VLAN - one shared network segment for devices - that can reach the internet. A login from a new source plus a new process on a camera is already strange - cameras rarely start new programs
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Post office opens
steps.caption: Malware on the camera opens an MQTT CONNECT to the attacker broker mqtt.badstream[.]net (198.51.100.90) on port 1883. From this moment the device has a live command channel. Cameras should never speak MQTT to the internet. TCP/1883 egress from the IoT VLAN is the first alarm
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Subscribe to orders
steps.caption: The implant subscribes to the topic cmd/cam-17 and waits silently. A subscription carries no message body, so the quiet connection pattern is the tell, not the traffic volume. An idle connection with a 60-second keepalive from a camera deserves a look
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Heartbeat publish
steps.caption: Every 60 seconds the camera publishes a small status message with uptime and load to stat/cam-17. This proves the channel works. Periodic small publishes from one device look exactly like a beacon - a regular signal that shows malware is alive. Measure the cadence per host
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Order arrives
steps.caption: The attacker publishes a command to cmd/cam-17: scan the local network 192.168.8.0/24 for new targets. The broker is the command injection point. Broker-side topic ACLs would stop a write from an untrusted client
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Results flow back
steps.caption: The camera publishes scan results to data/cam-17. It found 11 hosts and sends them in small chunks of a few kilobytes. Data topics can carry stolen files. Size limits force chunking, so watch for many similar messages
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Odd port alert
steps.caption: The SIEM (security information and event management - the log platform the SOC watches) raises the rule for outbound 1883/8883 from the IoT VLAN. The analyst checks the destination: it is not on the broker allowlist. Allowlist known brokers only. Anything else on these ports is a candidate incident
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Close the post office
steps.caption: The team blocks 198.51.100.90 and the domain, rebuilds the camera from known firmware (the device's built-in software), moves the IoT VLAN to deny-by-default egress, and rotates device passwords. Fix the policy, not only the device - the next implant should find a closed door
